text.p: Dr. Jack Kevorkian dropped off the body of a 65-year-old woman at a hospital on Wednesday night and was detained by police who took his car, a lawyer for the assisted suicide crusader said on Thursday.

Barbara Collins of Falmouth, Massachusetts, was pronounced dead by William Beaumont Hospital emergency room workers shortly before 8 p.m. EDT (2400 GMT) on Wednesday, said Colette Stimmell, a spokeswoman for the hospital in Royal Oak, a suburb northwest of Detroit.
Collins, who suffered from terminal ovarian cancer, was the 44th person Kevorkian has admitted helping die since 1990.

Following hospital policy, Stimmell said, workers called Royal Oak police, who arrived about the time Kevorkian was leaving. Geoffrey Fieger, one of Kevorkian's attorneys, said police forced Kevorkian from his car and wrestled his keys away, bruising him in the process.

"They beat him. They rousted him out of his automobile. They stole his car," Fieger said. He said Kevorkian was forced to call Fieger's wife to pick him up at the hospital. He added that police refused to say why they took the car.
Royal Oak police officials could not be reached for comment on Thursday. Late on Wednesday, a spokesman refused to comment on the incident other than to say that Kevorkian was not arrested.

It was the second time in a week Kevorkian has clashed with Royal Oak police, prompting Fieger to repeat his charge that Oakland County Prosecutor Richard Thompson and law enforcement authorities were spying on and harassing the retired pathologist.
"They've apparently been given permission by Thompson to do whatever they have to do," he said.
Oakland County Medical Examiner Dr. Ljubisa Dragovic said on Thursday an autopsy confirmed Collins was terminally ill with ovarian cancer and had an estimated six months to live.
Dragovic said she was poisoned by an intravenous injection of a lethal substance. That makes her death a homicide because she was injected by someone else, Dragovic said.

Of the 38 Kevorkian-assisted suicides that his office has now handled, Dragovic said 10 were terminally ill to the point where death would have likely occurred in six months, 25 had physical incapacities but were not terminally ill and three showed no anatomical evidence of disease.
